title: Red leg: differentials & referral
summary: A structured approach to the red leg: is it really cellulitis? Bilateral, chronic, itchy redness is usually venous. Plus a one-table guide to when to refer urgently.

glance.think: Any patient presenting with ‘cellulitis’, especially if both legs are involved, it is chronic or itchy, or there is no fever.
glance.engine: Most bilateral red legs are venous (stasis dermatitis, lipodermatosclerosis) or oedema, not infection.
glance.backbone: Ask: one leg or two, acute or chronic, fever or not, itch or pain? Treat the actual cause.
glance.never_miss: Necrotising fasciitis, sepsis, DVT, critical ischaemia and diabetic foot infection.

what: ‘Red leg’ is a presentation, not a diagnosis. Up to a third of patients admitted with ‘cellulitis’ turn out to have a **mimic** (pseudocellulitis). This page brings together the Module 5 red-leg teaching and the referral triggers for leg ulcers.

head: Clue
Points towards
rows: Painful, woody, red gaiter skin, often bilateral
Calf swelling and tenderness, less skin redness
Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, toxic

features: Compare the photos below. Venous eczema is scaly and itchy on **both** legs. Lipodermatosclerosis is indurated and tapering. True cellulitis is hot, tender, **one-sided** and expanding.

list: Ask: **one leg or two?** Acute or chronic? Fever or rigors? Itch or pain? Is there a portal of entry?
Mark the border and record observations (NEWS2).
Wells score with D-dimer or Doppler if DVT is possible.
Check pulses or ABPI if there is an ulcer, or before compression.

head: Mimic
Distinguishing clues
rows: Bilateral or chronic, itchy, scale, haemosiderin, no fever
Painful, woody, red skin above the ankle, often misdiagnosed as cellulitis
Calf pain and swelling, less intense redness
Itchy, vesicular, matches the area covered
**Severe pain out of proportion**, rapid progression, systemic toxicity. **ED**
Ulcer edge features, purpura, systemic disease

head: Situation
Action
rows: Facial or orbital cellulitis, or rapidly spreading
Critical limb ischaemia, rest pain or gangrene
Leg ulcer not improving, or atypical edge
Tissue viability plus dermatology or vascular
Red leg with no fever, bilateral, chronic and itchy
Rethink: venous eczema. Emollient, topical steroid and compression, **no antibiotic**
Treat portals of entry; discuss prophylaxis with a clinician

red_flags: Pain out of proportion, purple bullae, crepitus, or a rapidly spreading area: **necrotising fasciitis**.
Sepsis signs: low blood pressure, tachycardia, confusion, mottling.
A cold, pulseless or ischaemic limb.
A diabetic foot that is hot, red or ulcerated.
pearls: Venous eczema responds to emollient plus a topical steroid and compression (after ABPI). Antibiotics do nothing for it.
Recurrent ‘cellulitis’ in the same leg may be lipodermatosclerosis. Look at the whole leg history.
